title: Meet your cosmic neighbourhood
markdown:
Imagine leaving your house, then your city, then Earth. Zoom out far enough and our home becomes one small member of a much bigger neighbourhood: the **solar system**.

At its heart is the **Sun**, a star. Eight planets travel around it: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. Planets do not make their own starlight; we see them because they reflect sunlight.

## Read the picture
The glowing object on the left is the Sun. Moving right takes you through the planets in order. This is a map of *order*, not distance: real space has enormous gaps, and the planets are not lined up like this.

The family includes moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets too. Our Moon travels around Earth while Earth travels around the Sun. Think of a smaller journey happening inside a larger one.

You now have the basic map. Next comes the surprising question: why don't these worlds simply drift away?
takeaway: The solar system is the Sun and the worlds and smaller objects bound to it by gravity.
next: Why planets keep moving around the Sun
summary: Introduced the Sun as a star, eight planets in order, Earth third, reflected sunlight, moons and smaller bodies. Diagram is not to scale.

diagram.caption: The eight planets in order. Sizes, spacing and alignment are illustrative, not to scale.

title: An orbit is a continuous turn
markdown:
Throw a ball gently and it falls nearby. Throw it harder and it travels farther before landing. In an ideal world without air or obstacles, enough sideways speed would let it keep falling *around* Earth. That is the idea behind an **orbit**.

## Two things happen together
A planet already has motion through space. Meanwhile, the Sun's gravity pulls it inward. Gravity is the attraction between things that have mass—the amount of matter they contain.

Without gravity, the planet would continue along a straight path. With gravity, its direction keeps changing. It follows a curved path around the Sun instead. The picture separates these two ideas so you can see how they work together.

There is no physical track, rail or string holding Earth up. Its orbit is motion shaped by gravity. Actual planetary paths are slightly stretched circles called **ellipses**.

Think of orbiting as a journey that keeps turning. The planet is not parked in space; it is continually moving.
takeaway: Sideways motion and gravity together produce an orbit.
next: Why the inner and outer planets are so different
summary: Explained orbit as motion curved by gravity, continuous falling, mass and elliptical paths. No rails or physical strings.

diagram.caption: A simplified orbit viewed from above. The blue arrow shows motion; the gold arrow shows the inward pull of gravity. Not to scale.

title: Two very different kinds of neighbourhood
markdown:
Imagine choosing where to land a spacecraft. Earth and Jupiter are both planets—but they offer very different destinations.

## The rocky worlds
**Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars** are the inner planets. They have solid, rocky surfaces. You could, in principle, place a lander on their ground, although the conditions can be extremely hostile.

## The giant worlds
Farther out are four giant planets. **Jupiter and Saturn** are gas giants. **Uranus and Neptune** are ice giants, a name related to their composition, not a promise of a frozen surface you could walk on. They have no solid surface like Earth's; descending means entering deeper atmospheric layers under increasing pressure.

This makes “planet” a broad family name, not a guarantee that every member resembles home. The picture groups the eight worlds by their basic structure.

When you hear about a mission to another planet, ask a useful question: will it fly past, orbit, descend into an atmosphere, or land? The planet's structure helps determine which of those adventures is possible.
takeaway: The inner four planets are rocky; the outer four are giants without an Earth-like solid surface.

summary: Distinguished rocky inner worlds, gas giants Jupiter/Saturn, ice giants Uranus/Neptune, and implications for spacecraft.
